"Two-panel diagram showing RB gene function. Panel 1 'Normal RB Function': hypophosphorylated RB protein binding E2F labeled 'RB binds E2F — cell cannot pass G1 to S phase — controlled division.' Panel 2 'RB Inactivated': RB lost with red X → E2F unblocked and active → cell passes G1-S freely → uncontrolled division → bladder, breast, lung cancer icons. Car analogy inset: 'RB = Governor of the Cell Cycle.' No title above. No summary box below. Flat vector diagram. White background."

Caption:
The RB protein acts as the cell cycle's governor — when active it blocks E2F transcription factors from pushing the cell into division. Loss of RB, seen in bladder, breast and lung cancers, removes this brake and allows unchecked cell proliferation.

illustrae.name:
"Two-pathway diagram showing TP53 function and loss. Top pathway 'Normal TP53 Function': DNA damage → ATM/ATR kinase phosphorylates p53 → MDM2 released → p53 activates two outcomes: p21 causing G1-S checkpoint arrest, and apoptosis if damage irreparable. Bottom pathway 'Loss of TP53': mutated TP53 red X → cell replicates despite damage → no apoptosis → cancer. Statistics box: TP53 mutated in up to 50% of all cancers. List: leukemias, lymphomas, sarcomas, brain tumors, breast, colon, lung. No title above. No summary box below. Flat vector diagram. White background."

Caption:
TP53 normally detects DNA damage and either pauses the cell cycle for repair or triggers cell death. When TP53 is mutated — which occurs in nearly half of all cancers — damaged cells survive and divide uncontrollably.

illustrae.name:
Four-panel educational diagram showing the four major DNA repair pathways. Panel 1 'Base Excision Repair (BER)': DNA strand with one damaged base flipped out of helix labeled 'Base flipping.' DNA glycosylase removing single damaged base labeled 'Cuts bond between base and deoxyribose.' Gap labeled 'Apurinic or apyrimidinic site.' New correct base inserted and sealed. Panel 2 'Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)': DNA strand with two fused thymine bases labeled 'Pyrimidine dimer — UV radiation.' Nuclease cutting out damaged section. Polymerase filling gap. Ligase sealing strand. Panel 3 'Mismatch Repair (MMR)': mismatched base pair causing helix distortion labeled 'Mismatch detected.' Repair proteins removing and replacing wrong base. Note: 'Inherited MMR defects increase cancer predisposition.' Panel 4 'Double-Strand Break Repair (DSBR)': both strands completely broken labeled 'DSB — ionizing radiation or replication errors.' ATM kinase labeled 'Detects DSB — activates repair signaling.' Two branches: Homologous recombination (precise) and Non-homologous end joining (error prone). No title above image. No summary box below. Flat vector diagram. White background. Clean leader lines. Scientific oncology textbook style."

caption
DNA repair pathways protect the genome from damage. Base excision repair removes single damaged bases, nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions caused by UV radiation, mismatch repair corrects replication errors, and double-strand break repair fixes complete breaks in both DNA strands. Defects in any of these pathways can lead to genomic instability and cancer development.
